Guyana: Beyond the Social Media Hype — A Personal Reflection
I recently visited Guyana, a country that has received considerable attention and praise on social media. Given all the hype surrounding its development and future prospects, I arrived with certain expectations. However, I left feeling surprised, shocked, and disappointed all at the same time.
What I observed led me to question whether Guyana is truly moving in the direction of meaningful and sustainable progress. In my view, the country exhibits characteristics of an authoritarian culture that appears to begin at the highest levels of government and trickle down through various levels of society, particularly among those in positions of authority. The result, as I experienced it, is a system in which people are often subjected to the misuse of authority, not necessarily through direct government intervention in every instance, but through an entrenched culture that can foster hostility, indifference, and a lack of genuine friendliness toward others.
Despite all the excitement and optimism surrounding Guyana, I struggle to envision a bright future for a society in which people appear constrained by systemic problems and where there seems to be insufficient emphasis on innovation, critical thinking, and a shared vision for progress.
Georgetown, in particular, left me deeply concerned. Many buildings and houses appeared dilapidated, with some seemingly untouched by a fresh coat of paint for decades. In certain areas, stagnant water collected in roadside drains, producing unpleasant odors and raising serious concerns about public health and sanitation. What astonished me most was seeing people going about their daily lives amid these conditions, seemingly accustomed to an environment that, in my opinion, demands urgent attention. When poor sanitation becomes normalized, the danger is that a serious public health concern may no longer be recognized as the crisis it is.
The city’s infrastructure raised further questions. Many streets are narrow, and traffic lights, clearly marked road dividers, and adequate signage appear insufficient in certain areas. These are not merely cosmetic concerns; they affect road safety, urban mobility, and the overall quality of life.
The journey from Cheddi Jagan International Airport to Georgetown is another example of the challenges facing the country. Although the distance is approximately 26 to 30 miles by road, the trip can sometimes take two and a half to three hours, depending on traffic and road conditions. The road infrastructure is inadequate in places, and sections of the journey, particularly closer to the airport, can feel more like a rough track than a major route connecting an international airport to the nation’s capital.
Poor urban planning could make these challenges even more difficult to resolve in the future. Many buildings have been constructed close to the roadway, leaving limited space for widening roads or improving transportation infrastructure. More concerning is the possibility that the same pattern of development will continue if building permits are granted without adequate setbacks and long-term planning. Decisions made today can create infrastructure problems that become significantly more expensive, disruptive, or even impractical to correct tomorrow.
Vision is the foundation of meaningful progress. Development requires more than economic growth, public announcements, or optimistic social media narratives. It requires thoughtful planning, competent leadership, accountability, investment in infrastructure, and a commitment to improving the everyday lives of ordinary citizens.
For Guyana to realize its full potential, I believe it must confront the cultural and institutional barriers that discourage independent thought, initiative, and innovation. People must be empowered to think critically, challenge outdated practices, develop their abilities, and contribute meaningfully to the improvement of their communities. A society cannot reach its full potential when its people feel constrained by authority or discouraged from thinking and acting independently.
I also observed what appeared to be an emphasis on government as the principal source of solutions and progress. Yet no government, regardless of its resources or ambitions, can build a truly prosperous nation on its own. Sustainable development depends on an educated, empowered, and innovative population. Government’s responsibility is not simply to convince people that it can create everything; it is to create the conditions in which citizens can develop their talents, establish businesses, solve problems, and improve their own circumstances. This requires education, incentives, opportunity, and institutions that reward initiative and excellence.
Ultimately, natural resources and economic growth alone do not guarantee national progress. Without a clear vision, sound planning, strong institutions, civic responsibility, and a population equipped to think independently and innovate, a country risks missing the opportunity to transform its wealth into lasting prosperity.
Guyana has potential, but potential is not the same as progress. The real measure of development is not simply how much wealth a country generates, but how effectively that wealth translates into better infrastructure, healthier communities, stronger institutions, greater individual opportunity, and an improved quality of life for its people.
These are some of my observations from my recent visit to Guyana. They are the impressions of a visitor who arrived amid considerable public enthusiasm but left with serious questions about the country’s direction. I hope Guyana will confront these challenges honestly and pursue a path that places long-term planning, education, accountability, innovation, and the well-being of its people at the center of national development.
A country’s future is not determined by its natural resources alone, but by the vision, leadership, and people who shape what it becomes.
